title: Physics National Model Exam 3 2024
description: Physics National Model Exam 3 2024 featuring 100 authentic questions with step-by-step solutions. Designed for Ethiopian national exam mastery.

questions.questionText: A liquid is contained in a vessel open to the atmosphere. Which factor directly determines the gauge pressure at a point below the liquid surface?
options: The density of the liquid and its depth below the surface
Only the total volume of the liquid
The shape of the container and the surface area
questions.explanation:
The gauge pressure in a liquid at rest is given by P = ρgh.

Therefore, it depends on the density of the liquid, the acceleration due to gravity, and the depth below the liquid surface.

It does not depend on the shape of the container.

questions.questionText: Water flows through a horizontal pipe whose cross-sectional area decreases from A₁ to A₂. If the flow is steady and incompressible, the speed of the water in the narrower section is
options: smaller than its speed in the wider section.
greater than its speed in the wider section.
questions.explanation:
For steady incompressible flow, the equation of continuity is A₁v₁ = A₂v₂.

When the cross-sectional area decreases, the velocity must increase so that the same volume of fluid passes through the pipe per unit time.

Therefore, water moves faster in the narrower section.

questions.questionText: According to Bernoulli's principle, when the speed of a fluid increases along a horizontal streamline, its pressure generally
questions.explanation:
For steady ideal flow along a horizontal streamline, Bernoulli's equation gives P + ½ρv² = constant.

Therefore, an increase in fluid speed is associated with a decrease in pressure when the height remains unchanged.

questions.questionText: A liquid of density 800 kg/m³ is contained in a tank. What is the gauge pressure at a depth of 2.5 m below its surface? Take g = 10 m/s².
questions.explanation:
The gauge pressure is P = ρgh.

Substituting ρ = 800 kg/m³, g = 10 m/s², and h = 2.5 m gives

P = 800 × 10 × 2.5 = 20,000 Pa.

Therefore, the gauge pressure is 20,000 Pa.

questions.questionText: Two points inside the same liquid are at different depths. Which statement about their hydrostatic pressures is correct?
options: The deeper point always has lower pressure.
Both points must have exactly the same pressure.
The deeper point has greater pressure.
Pressure depends only on the surface area of the container.
questions.explanation:
The hydrostatic gauge pressure is P = ρgh.

For the same liquid, density and gravitational acceleration are the same, so pressure increases directly with depth.

Therefore, the deeper point has greater pressure.

questions.questionText: A planet moves around the Sun in an elliptical orbit. According to Kepler's second law, the line joining the planet to the Sun sweeps out
options: equal areas in equal time intervals.
equal distances in equal time intervals.
larger areas when the planet is closer to the Sun.
questions.explanation:
Kepler's second law states that a line joining a planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals.

This means that a planet moves faster when it is closer to the Sun and slower when it is farther away.

questions.questionText: A satellite moves around a planet in a circular orbit. If its orbital radius is increased while the mass of the central planet remains unchanged, its orbital speed will
questions.explanation:
For a circular orbit, the orbital speed is v = √(GM/r).

Thus, orbital speed is inversely proportional to the square root of the orbital radius.

Therefore, increasing the orbital radius decreases the orbital speed.

questions.questionText: A satellite has an orbital period of 8 hours around a planet. If another satellite has four times the orbital radius, what is its orbital period assuming the same central planet?
questions.explanation:
Kepler's third law gives T² ∝ R³.

Therefore, T₂/T₁ = (R₂/R₁)^(3/2).

For R₂ = 4R₁,

T₂/T₁ = 4^(3/2) = 8.

Thus, T₂ = 8 × 8 = 64 hours.

Therefore, the correct option is 2.

questions.questionText: A vector has components 6 m along the positive x-axis and 8 m along the positive y-axis. What is its magnitude?
questions.explanation:
The magnitude of a vector with perpendicular components is A = √(Aₓ² + Aᵧ²).

Therefore, A = √(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10 m.

questions.questionText: Two vectors A⃗ and B⃗ have magnitudes 5 and 4 respectively, and the angle between them is 60°. What is their dot product?
questions.explanation:
The dot product is A⃗ · B⃗ = AB cosθ.

Therefore,

A⃗ · B⃗ = 5 × 4 × cos60° = 20 × 0.5 = 10.

questions.questionText: Two vectors have a dot product equal to zero. If neither vector has zero magnitude, the angle between them must be
questions.explanation:
The dot product is A⃗ · B⃗ = AB cosθ.

If both vectors are non-zero and their dot product is zero, then cosθ = 0.

Therefore, θ = 90°, meaning the vectors are perpendicular.

questions.questionText: An object moves from position x = 2 m to position x = -5 m along a straight line. What is its displacement?
questions.explanation:
Displacement is final position minus initial position.

Δx = x_f - x_i = -5 - 2 = -7 m.

The negative sign indicates displacement toward the negative x-direction.

questions.questionText: A car initially traveling at 10 m/s accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s² for 5 seconds. What is its final velocity?
questions.explanation:
For uniform acceleration, v = u + at.

Here, u = 10 m/s, a = 2 m/s², and t = 5 s.

Therefore, v = 10 + (2)(5) = 20 m/s.

questions.questionText: An object starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 4 m/s². What distance does it travel during the first 3 seconds?
questions.explanation:
The displacement under uniform acceleration is s = ut + ½at².

Since the object starts from rest, u = 0.

Therefore, s = ½(4)(3²) = 18 m.

questions.questionText: A stone is thrown vertically upward with an initial speed of 20 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s², what is the maximum height reached by the stone?
questions.explanation:
At maximum height, the final velocity is zero.

Using v² = u² + 2as,

0 = 20² - 2(10)h.

Therefore, h = 400/20 = 20 m.

questions.questionText: A ball is thrown horizontally from the top of a cliff. Ignoring air resistance, its horizontal velocity during the flight
questions.explanation:
In ideal projectile motion, there is no horizontal acceleration when air resistance is neglected.

Therefore, the horizontal component of velocity remains constant throughout the flight.

questions.questionText: A projectile is launched at an angle of 45° above the horizontal with a fixed initial speed. At the highest point of its path, its vertical velocity is
options: equal to its initial vertical velocity.
greater than its initial vertical velocity.
questions.explanation:
At the highest point of projectile motion, the vertical component of velocity becomes zero.

The horizontal component remains constant if air resistance is neglected.

Therefore, the vertical velocity at the highest point is zero.

questions.questionText: A 10 kg object is acted upon by a net force of 50 N. What is its acceleration?
questions.explanation:
Newton's second law states that F = ma.

Therefore, a = F/m = 50/10 = 5 m/s².

questions.questionText: A 4 kg object is moving with a velocity of 6 m/s. What is its linear momentum?
questions.explanation:
Linear momentum is p = mv.

Therefore, p = 4 × 6 = 24 kg·m/s.

questions.questionText: A constant force of 15 N acts in the same direction as the displacement of an object through 4 m. How much work is done by the force?
questions.explanation:
Work done by a constant force is W = Fd cosθ.

Since the force and displacement are in the same direction, θ = 0° and cos0° = 1.

Therefore, W = 15 × 4 = 60 J.

questions.questionText: A machine performs 900 J of useful work in 30 seconds. What is its average power output?
questions.explanation:
Average power is P = W/t.

Therefore, P = 900/30 = 30 W.

questions.questionText: A 2 kg object is moving at 10 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
questions.explanation:
Kinetic energy is KE = ½mv².

Therefore, KE = ½(2)(10²) = 100 J.

questions.questionText: A body is raised vertically through a height of 5 m. If its mass is 6 kg and g = 10 m/s², what is the increase in gravitational potential energy?
questions.explanation:
The change in gravitational potential energy is ΔPE = mgh.

Therefore, ΔPE = 6 × 10 × 5 = 300 J.

questions.questionText: A block slides across a rough horizontal surface and eventually comes to rest. The work done by friction on the block is
options: positive because friction increases its speed.
negative because friction removes mechanical energy.
zero because friction is perpendicular to displacement.
always equal to the initial kinetic energy with a positive sign.
questions.explanation:
Friction acts opposite to the direction of motion.

Therefore, the angle between friction and displacement is 180°, making the work done by friction negative.

The negative work represents the removal of mechanical energy.

questions.questionText: A 5 kg block rests on a horizontal surface. If the coefficient of static friction is 0.4 and g = 10 m/s², what is the maximum static friction force?
questions.explanation:
The maximum static friction is f_s,max = μ_sN.

On a horizontal surface, N = mg = 5 × 10 = 50 N.

Therefore, f_s,max = 0.4 × 50 = 20 N.

questions.questionText: A 20 N force is applied to a 4 kg block on a frictionless horizontal surface. What is the acceleration of the block?
questions.explanation:
Using Newton's second law, F = ma.

Therefore, a = F/m = 20/4 = 5 m/s².

questions.questionText: A 2 kg object moves in a circle of radius 0.5 m with a speed of 4 m/s. What is its centripetal acceleration?
questions.explanation:
Centripetal acceleration is a_c = v²/r.

Therefore, a_c = 4²/0.5 = 16/0.5 = 32 m/s².

questions.questionText: A wheel rotates at an angular speed of 10 rad/s. What is the linear speed of a point located 0.3 m from its axis?
questions.explanation:
The relationship between linear and angular speed is v = ωr.

Therefore, v = 10 × 0.3 = 3 m/s.

questions.questionText: A rotating body has a moment of inertia of 4 kg·m² and an angular acceleration of 3 rad/s². What net torque acts on the body?
questions.explanation:
Rotational Newton's second law is τ = Iα.

Therefore, τ = 4 × 3 = 12 N·m.

questions.questionText: A uniform beam is in rotational equilibrium. Which condition must be satisfied?
options: The net torque about any suitable point is zero.
Every individual torque must be zero.
The beam must have zero mass.
The angular velocity must continuously increase.
questions.explanation:
Rotational equilibrium requires the algebraic sum of all torques about a point to be zero.

Thus, ∑τ = 0.

Individual torques do not necessarily have to be zero because clockwise and counterclockwise torques can balance each other.

questions.questionText: A metal rod is heated and its temperature increases by 50 °C. If its original length is 2 m and its coefficient of linear expansion is 2 × 10⁻⁵ °C⁻¹, what is its increase in length?
questions.explanation:
Linear expansion is given by ΔL = αL₀ΔT.

Therefore, ΔL = (2 × 10⁻⁵)(2)(50) = 0.002 m.

questions.questionText: A substance absorbs 5000 J of heat while its temperature increases by 20 °C. If its mass is 2 kg, what is its specific heat capacity?
questions.explanation:
Specific heat capacity is determined from Q = mcΔT.

Therefore, c = Q/(mΔT) = 5000/(2 × 20) = 125 J/kg·°C.

Thus, the correct numerical value is 125 J/kg·°C, which corresponds to option 1.

questions.questionText: A 0.5 kg aluminum block has a specific heat capacity of 900 J/kg·°C. How much heat is needed to increase its temperature by 20 °C?
questions.explanation:
Using Q = mcΔT,

Q = 0.5 × 900 × 20 = 9000 J.

Therefore, 9000 J of heat is required.

questions.questionText: When a substance changes from a liquid to a gas at constant temperature, the heat supplied is mainly used to
options: increase the temperature of the liquid.
increase the mass of the substance.
overcome intermolecular forces and change its phase.
decrease the internal energy of the substance.
questions.explanation:
During a phase change, the temperature remains constant while the supplied heat changes the internal structure of the substance.

During vaporization, energy is used mainly to overcome intermolecular attractions and separate the particles.

questions.questionText: Which change of state occurs when a gas changes directly into a solid without becoming a liquid?
questions.explanation:
Deposition is the direct change from a gas to a solid without passing through the liquid state.

The reverse process, solid directly to gas, is called sublimation.

questions.questionText: The temperature at which a liquid's vapor pressure becomes equal to the surrounding atmospheric pressure is called its
questions.explanation:
A liquid boils when its vapor pressure becomes equal to the external pressure.

Therefore, the boiling point depends on the surrounding pressure.

questions.questionText: If the external pressure on a liquid is increased, its boiling temperature generally
questions.explanation:
A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the surrounding pressure.

A higher external pressure requires a higher temperature for the vapor pressure to reach that value.

Therefore, the boiling temperature increases.

questions.questionText: A gas occupies 2.0 L at constant temperature and pressure. If its amount of gas is doubled while the temperature and pressure remain constant, its volume becomes
questions.explanation:
According to Avogadro's law, at constant temperature and pressure, volume is directly proportional to the amount of gas.

Doubling the amount of gas therefore doubles the volume.

V₂ = 2 × 2.0 = 4.0 L.

questions.questionText: A 12 V battery is connected to a resistor of resistance 4 Ω. What current flows through the resistor?
questions.explanation:
Ohm's law states V = IR.

Therefore, I = V/R = 12/4 = 3 A.

questions.questionText: Two resistors of 4 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in series. What is their equivalent resistance?
questions.explanation:
For resistors connected in series, the equivalent resistance is the sum of their resistances.

R_eq = 4 + 6 = 10 Ω.

questions.questionText: Two resistors of 6 Ω and 3 Ω are connected in parallel. What is their equivalent resistance?
questions.explanation:
For two resistors in parallel,

1/R_eq = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂.

Therefore, 1/R_eq = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2.

Thus, R_eq = 2 Ω.

questions.questionText: A resistor carries a current of 2 A when connected across a potential difference of 10 V. What power is dissipated by the resistor?
questions.explanation:
Electrical power is P = VI.

Therefore, P = 10 × 2 = 20 W.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly describes Kirchhoff's junction rule?
options: The sum of currents entering a junction equals the sum of currents leaving it.
The voltage across every resistor must be zero.
The resistance of every branch must be equal.
The current must always flow clockwise around a circuit.
questions.explanation:
Kirchhoff's current law follows from conservation of electric charge.

At any junction, the total current entering must equal the total current leaving.

Therefore, the algebraic sum of currents at a junction is zero.

questions.questionText: A capacitor is charged to a potential difference V. If the potential difference is increased while its capacitance remains constant, the charge stored on the capacitor
questions.explanation:
The charge stored by a capacitor is Q = CV.

If capacitance remains constant, increasing the potential difference causes the stored charge to increase proportionally.

questions.questionText: A capacitor has a capacitance of 5 μF and is connected to a 20 V source. What charge does it store?
questions.explanation:
The charge stored by a capacitor is Q = CV.

Q = (5 × 10⁻⁶)(20) = 100 × 10⁻⁶ C = 100 μC.

questions.questionText: When a dielectric is inserted between the plates of an isolated charged capacitor, the capacitance increases. What happens to the potential difference between the plates?
questions.explanation:
For an isolated capacitor, the charge remains constant.

Since Q = CV, increasing the capacitance causes the potential difference V = Q/C to decrease.

Therefore, the potential difference decreases.

questions.questionText: A positive point charge is placed in an electric field. The electric force on the charge acts
options: opposite to the electric field direction.
in the direction of the electric field.
only when the charge is moving.
questions.explanation:
The electric field direction is defined as the direction of the force acting on a positive test charge.

Therefore, a positive charge experiences force in the direction of the electric field.

questions.questionText: Two positive point charges are brought closer to each other. The magnitude of the electrostatic force between them
questions.explanation:
Coulomb's law gives F = k|q₁q₂|/r².

The force is inversely proportional to the square of the separation distance.

Therefore, decreasing the distance causes the force to increase.

questions.questionText: Two point charges of 2 μC and 3 μC are separated by 0.3 m in vacuum. What is the approximate electrostatic force between them? Take k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C².
questions.explanation:
Using Coulomb's law,

F = kq₁q₂/r².

F = (9 × 10⁹)(2 × 10⁻⁶)(3 × 10⁻⁶)/(0.3)².

Therefore, F = 0.6 N.

questions.questionText: A long straight wire carries an electric current. If the current is doubled while the distance from the wire remains unchanged, the magnetic field strength becomes
questions.explanation:
For a long straight current-carrying wire, the magnetic field is B = μ₀I/(2πr).

At constant distance, magnetic field is directly proportional to current.

Therefore, doubling the current doubles the magnetic field.

questions.questionText: The magnetic field produced by a long straight current-carrying wire is directed
options: in circular paths around the wire.
questions.explanation:
The magnetic field around a long straight current-carrying wire forms concentric circular paths centered on the wire.

Its direction can be determined using the right-hand grip rule.

questions.questionText: A charged particle moves parallel to a uniform magnetic field. What is the magnetic force acting on the particle?
questions.explanation:
The magnetic force is F = |q|vBsinθ.

When the particle moves parallel to the magnetic field, θ = 0° and sin0° = 0.

Therefore, the magnetic force is zero.

questions.questionText: A proton enters a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to its velocity. If the magnetic field strength is increased while the proton speed remains constant, the magnetic force
questions.explanation:
The magnetic force magnitude is F = qvBsinθ.

For perpendicular motion, sin90° = 1, so F = qvB.

Therefore, increasing B increases the magnetic force.

questions.questionText: A coil experiences a changing magnetic flux. According to Faraday's law, the magnitude of the induced emf is related to the
options: rate of change of magnetic flux.
questions.explanation:
Faraday's law states that the magnitude of induced emf is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux through the coil.

For N turns, the magnitude is |ε| = N|dΦ/dt|.

questions.questionText: A magnet is moved rapidly toward a conducting coil. Compared with moving the same magnet slowly toward the coil, the rapidly moving magnet produces
options: the same induced emf in all cases.
questions.explanation:
Faraday's law states that induced emf depends on the rate of change of magnetic flux.

Moving the magnet more rapidly produces a greater rate of flux change.

Therefore, a larger induced emf is produced.

questions.questionText: A transformer has 100 turns in its primary coil and 500 turns in its secondary coil. If the primary voltage is 20 V, what is the ideal secondary voltage?
questions.explanation:
For an ideal transformer,

Vₚ/Vₛ = Nₚ/Nₛ.

Therefore, Vₛ = Vₚ(Nₛ/Nₚ) = 20(500/100) = 100 V.

The secondary voltage is therefore 100 V.

questions.questionText: A transformer has more turns in its secondary coil than in its primary coil. Such a transformer is generally called a
questions.explanation:
For an ideal transformer, voltage is proportional to the number of turns.

If the secondary has more turns than the primary, the secondary voltage is greater.

Therefore, it is a step-up transformer.

questions.questionText: A ray of light passes from glass into air. If the angle of incidence is increased beyond the critical angle, the light undergoes
questions.explanation:
When light travels from a denser medium to a less dense medium, total internal reflection occurs if the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle.

The light is then reflected completely back into the denser medium.

questions.questionText: A convex lens has a focal length of 20 cm. An object is placed 60 cm from the lens. What type of image is formed?
questions.explanation:
For a convex lens, when the object is placed beyond twice the focal length, a real and inverted image is formed between f and 2f.

Here, 2f = 40 cm and the object is at 60 cm.

Therefore, the image is real and inverted.

questions.questionText: An object is placed between a convex lens and its focal point. The image produced is
questions.explanation:
When an object is placed between the focal point and the optical center of a convex lens, the refracted rays diverge.

Their backward extensions meet on the same side as the object, producing a virtual, upright, and magnified image.

questions.questionText: Which type of lens is commonly used to correct short-sightedness, or myopia?
questions.explanation:
In myopia, distant objects are focused in front of the retina.

A concave lens diverges incoming rays before they enter the eye, allowing the eye lens to focus the image correctly on the retina.

questions.questionText: Which type of lens is used to correct long-sightedness, or hyperopia?
questions.explanation:
In hyperopia, light from nearby objects would be focused behind the retina.

A convex lens converges the incoming rays and helps the eye form the image on the retina.

questions.questionText: A concave mirror forms a real, inverted image of the same size as the object when the object is placed
options: between the pole and focal point.
questions.explanation:
For a concave mirror, an object placed at the center of curvature produces a real, inverted image at the center of curvature.

The image has the same size as the object.

questions.questionText: Two plane mirrors are inclined at 90° to each other. If an object is placed between them under the usual symmetric arrangement, how many images are formed?
questions.explanation:
For two plane mirrors inclined at angle θ, when 360°/θ is an integer, the number of images is n = 360°/θ - 1.

For θ = 90°,

n = 360/90 - 1 = 4 - 1 = 3 images.

questions.questionText: The resolving power of an optical instrument is mainly related to its ability to
options: distinguish between two closely spaced objects.
increase the mass of an object.
questions.explanation:
Resolving power refers to the ability of an optical instrument to distinguish two objects that are very close together as separate objects.

A higher resolving power means finer details can be distinguished.

questions.questionText: A refracting telescope has an objective lens with a long focal length and an eyepiece with a short focal length. The main purpose of the objective lens is to
options: produce sound from the distant object.
collect light and form the initial image.
reduce the wavelength of light to zero.
questions.explanation:
The objective lens of a refracting telescope collects light from a distant object and forms a real image near its focal plane.

The eyepiece then magnifies this image for observation.

questions.questionText: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and a wavelength of 4 m. What is its speed?
questions.explanation:
Wave speed is given by v = fλ.

Therefore, v = 50 × 4 = 200 m/s.

questions.questionText: A wave travels at 300 m/s and has a frequency of 100 Hz. What is its wavelength?
questions.explanation:
The wave relationship is v = fλ.

Therefore, λ = v/f = 300/100 = 3 m.

questions.questionText: If the frequency of a wave is doubled while its speed in the medium remains constant, its wavelength
questions.explanation:
From v = fλ, wavelength is λ = v/f.

If the wave speed remains constant and frequency doubles, the wavelength must become half as large.

questions.questionText: Which characteristic of a sound wave is most directly associated with the perceived loudness of the sound?
questions.explanation:
The loudness of a sound is related to the amplitude of the sound wave.

A larger amplitude generally corresponds to a louder sound, while frequency is mainly associated with pitch.

questions.questionText: The pitch of a musical sound is primarily determined by its
questions.explanation:
Pitch is the perception associated mainly with the frequency of a sound wave.

Higher frequency corresponds to higher pitch, while lower frequency corresponds to lower pitch.

questions.questionText: Which type of electromagnetic radiation has a shorter wavelength than visible violet light?
questions.explanation:
In the electromagnetic spectrum, ultraviolet radiation has a shorter wavelength and higher frequency than visible violet light.

Infrared, microwave, and radio waves have longer wavelengths than visible light.

questions.questionText: Which electromagnetic radiation generally has the highest frequency among the following?
questions.explanation:
Gamma rays occupy the highest-frequency, shortest-wavelength region of the electromagnetic spectrum.

Therefore, gamma rays have the highest frequency among the choices.

questions.questionText: A light wave has a frequency of 6 × 10¹⁴ Hz in vacuum. Taking the speed of light as 3 × 10⁸ m/s, what is its wavelength?
questions.explanation:
The speed of an electromagnetic wave is c = fλ.

Therefore,

λ = c/f = (3 × 10⁸)/(6 × 10¹⁴) = 0.5 × 10⁻⁶ m = 5 × 10⁻⁷ m.

questions.questionText: When white light passes through a prism, the separation of the different colors occurs because the refractive index of the material depends on
options: the mass of the prism only.
the electrical resistance of the prism.
questions.explanation:
Different wavelengths of light experience different refractive indices in a dispersive material.

Therefore, they bend by different amounts when passing through a prism, producing dispersion.

questions.questionText: A light ray enters glass from air at an angle of incidence of 30°. If the refractive index of glass is 1.5, which expression gives the sine of the refracted angle?
questions.explanation:
Using Snell's law, n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂.

For air, n₁ ≈ 1, so

sinθ₂ = sin30°/1.5 = 0.5/1.5 ≈ 0.33.

Therefore, sinθ is approximately 0.33.

questions.questionText: The work function of a metal is the minimum energy required to
options: stop an electron from moving inside the metal.
remove an electron from the surface of the metal.
increase the mass of a proton.
produce a neutron from an electron.
questions.explanation:
The work function is the minimum energy required to remove an electron from the surface of a metal.

In the photoelectric effect, photons must have at least this energy for electrons to be emitted.

questions.questionText: In the photoelectric effect, increasing the frequency of incident light above the threshold frequency generally causes the maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons to
questions.explanation:
Einstein's photoelectric equation is K_max = hf - φ.

Therefore, increasing the frequency increases the photon energy hf and consequently increases the maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons.

questions.questionText: The threshold frequency of a metal is the minimum frequency of incident radiation required to
options: heat the metal to its melting point.
produce visible light from the metal.
questions.explanation:
Threshold frequency is the minimum frequency of incident electromagnetic radiation that can eject electrons from a particular metal by the photoelectric effect.

Below this frequency, photoelectron emission does not occur regardless of intensity.

questions.questionText: Which particle is emitted during beta-minus radioactive decay?
questions.explanation:
In beta-minus decay, a neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton while emitting an electron and an antineutrino.

The emitted electron is called a beta-minus particle.

questions.questionText: During alpha decay of a radioactive nucleus, the mass number of the daughter nucleus decreases by
questions.explanation:
An alpha particle consists of two protons and two neutrons.

Therefore, emission of an alpha particle reduces the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2.

questions.questionText: A radioactive substance has a half-life of 6 hours. What fraction of the original nuclei remains after 18 hours?
questions.explanation:
The elapsed time is 18 hours, which corresponds to three half-lives.

After one half-life, 1/2 remains.

After two, 1/4 remains.

After three, 1/8 remains.

Therefore, one-eighth of the original nuclei remains.

questions.questionText: Which radiation has the greatest penetrating ability among alpha, beta, and gamma radiation?
options: All have exactly the same penetrating ability
questions.explanation:
Gamma radiation consists of high-energy electromagnetic waves and has much greater penetrating power than alpha or beta radiation.

Alpha particles are stopped by paper or the outer layer of skin, while beta particles have intermediate penetration.

questions.questionText: Nuclear fission refers to a process in which
options: two light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus.
heavy nucleus splits into smaller nuclei and releases energy.
an electron combines with a photon.
solid changes directly into a gas.
questions.explanation:
Nuclear fission occurs when a heavy nucleus splits into two or more lighter nuclei.

The process can release a large amount of energy and may also release additional neutrons capable of producing a chain reaction.

questions.questionText: Nuclear fusion is the process in which
options: heavy nucleus splits into smaller nuclei.
two or more light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus.
electrons are removed from an atom by light.
radioactive nucleus emits only gamma radiation.
questions.explanation:
Nuclear fusion involves combining light atomic nuclei to form a heavier nucleus.

A small amount of mass can be converted into a large amount of energy through E = mc².

questions.questionText: The mass of a bound atomic nucleus is generally less than the combined masses of its separated nucleons. This difference is called
questions.explanation:
The mass defect is the difference between the total mass of the separated nucleons and the actual mass of the bound nucleus.

The missing mass corresponds to nuclear binding energy through E = Δmc².

questions.questionText: If the mass defect of a nucleus is 0.01 u and 1 u corresponds to approximately 931 MeV, what is its binding energy?
questions.explanation:
The binding energy is E = Δmc².

Using the conversion 1 u ≈ 931 MeV,

E = 0.01 × 931 = 9.31 MeV.

questions.questionText: In a semiconductor, adding a small amount of impurity atoms to control its electrical conductivity is called
questions.explanation:
Doping is the intentional addition of impurity atoms to a semiconductor to modify its electrical conductivity.

Depending on the impurity, either n-type or p-type semiconductor material can be produced.

questions.questionText: A semiconductor doped with atoms that provide additional free electrons is classified as
questions.explanation:
Donor impurities contribute extra electrons to the semiconductor.

Such material is called n-type semiconductor because electrons are the majority charge carriers.

questions.questionText: In a p-type semiconductor, the majority charge carriers are
questions.explanation:
In p-type semiconductors, acceptor impurities create vacancies in the valence band called holes.

Holes therefore act as the majority charge carriers.

questions.questionText: A transistor is commonly used in electronic circuits as a
questions.explanation:
Transistors are fundamental semiconductor devices.

They can operate as electronic switches and can also amplify electrical signals when properly biased.

questions.questionText: In a bipolar junction transistor, the emitter is generally
options: lightly doped compared with the base.
heavily doped compared with the base.
questions.explanation:
The emitter is heavily doped so that it can inject a large number of charge carriers into the base.

The base is lightly doped, while the collector is generally moderately doped.

questions.questionText: Which transistor configuration is commonly used when a high voltage gain is required together with current gain?
questions.explanation:
The common-emitter configuration provides both current gain and voltage gain.

It is therefore widely used for signal amplification.

questions.questionText: Which logic gate produces a HIGH output only when both of its inputs are HIGH?
questions.explanation:
An AND gate gives a HIGH output only when all of its inputs are HIGH.

For two inputs, the output is 1 only for the combination A = 1 and B = 1.

questions.questionText: Which logic gate produces a LOW output only when both inputs are HIGH?
questions.explanation:
A NAND gate is the inverse of an AND gate.

Its output is LOW only when all inputs are HIGH.

For two inputs, the only LOW-output combination is A = 1 and B = 1.

questions.questionText: Which logic gate gives a HIGH output when at least one of its inputs is HIGH?
questions.explanation:
An OR gate produces a HIGH output when one or more of its inputs are HIGH.

For two inputs, its output is LOW only when both inputs are LOW.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a direct application of physics in medical diagnosis?
options: Using X-rays to produce images of internal body structures
questions.explanation:
Physics provides the principles behind many medical imaging technologies.

X-rays can pass through the body and produce images based on differences in absorption by different tissues.

questions.questionText: Which technology uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves to produce detailed images of internal body structures?
questions.explanation:
Magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, uses strong magnetic fields and radio-frequency waves to obtain detailed images of internal structures.

It does not use ionizing X-rays.

questions.questionText: Which physical quantity is conserved in an isolated system during an ordinary collision?
questions.explanation:
For an isolated system with no net external force, total linear momentum is conserved.

Kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions, not in all collisions.

questions.questionText: A 3 kg object moving at 4 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg object. If they stick together after collision, what is their common velocity?
questions.explanation:
For an isolated collision, momentum is conserved.

Initial momentum = 3 × 4 + 1 × 0 = 12 kg·m/s.

The combined mass is 4 kg.

Therefore, v = 12/4 = 3 m/s.
